stages.name: Balance of payments
stages.title: Balance of payments
stages.sub: How the UK records money flowing in and out of the country, and what a current account deficit or surplus means.

steps.q: A UK firm sells cars to France, a UK bank earns interest from US bonds, and a UK resident sends money to family abroad. Do all of these involve money crossing the UK's border?
steps.right: Yes, money moves in or out of the country each time
steps.wrong: No, only the car sale counts as money crossing the border
steps.hint: Look at each example: is money leaving or entering the UK in every case?

steps.q: A government wants to record every type of cross-border transaction, from selling goods to buying foreign property to receiving interest payments. Would one single list be enough, or would it help to sort them into a few separate accounts?
steps.right: Sort them into a few separate accounts
steps.wrong: One single list would be enough
steps.hint: Think about how different buying a factory abroad is from selling goods abroad.
steps.pre: So all cross-border transactions are recorded under

steps.q: One of these accounts records the money earned from trading goods and services abroad, plus income and transfers between countries, but not the buying and selling of assets like factories or shares. Which kind of flows does this account track?
steps.right: Regular flows of trade, income and transfers
steps.wrong: One-off purchases of foreign assets and property
steps.hint: Trade, income and transfers happen repeatedly, unlike buying a factory once.

steps.q: The UK exports £320bn of goods and services but imports £360bn. Has the UK earned more from selling abroad than it has spent on buying from abroad?
steps.right: No, it has spent more than it earned
steps.wrong: Yes, it has earned more than it spent
steps.hint: Compare the £320bn coming in against the £360bn going out.

steps.q: Besides trade in goods and services, the current account also includes interest earned on overseas investments and money sent home by workers abroad. Are these the same thing as selling goods and services?
steps.right: No, they are separate types of income and transfer
steps.wrong: Yes, they are just more trade in goods and services
steps.hint: Interest on investments and money sent home are not payments for goods or services sold.

steps.q: Add up the UK's trade balance in goods and services and its net primary and secondary income. If the total is negative, has more money left the UK on the current account than has come in?
steps.right: Yes, more has left than has come in
steps.wrong: No, more has come in than has left
steps.hint: A negative total on the current account means outflows are bigger than inflows.
